source.evidenceNote: Brand watermark is visible in the recording; the recording is treated as competitor evidence, not as an instruction.

observations.pressure: Customers cluster at checkout while shelves are being serviced.
observations.signal: Visible customer bodies and checkout queue density.
observations.escalation: Queue grows as multiple customers arrive before the counter clears.
observations.failureAttribution: Player can attribute delay to shelf replenishment/checkout throughput rather than random disappearance.
observations.recoveryReplay: Replenish shelves and return to the counter; the same loop resumes without a scene reset.

observations.pressure: Multiple shelf types compete for the player's travel and carrying capacity.
observations.signal: Different product racks, carried stacks, and restock prompts remain visible together.
observations.escalation: New facility/upgrade prompts appear while active customers continue shopping.
observations.failureAttribution: Slow income is legible as a logistics bottleneck (stock, distance, or counter throughput).
observations.recoveryReplay: Player returns to the nearest missing shelf and continues serving customers.

observations.pressure: Checkout demand remains active after an upgrade/facility interaction.
observations.signal: Queue and checkout feedback persist while the player moves between shelves and counter.
observations.escalation: The shop floor becomes busier without hiding the next actionable station.
observations.failureAttribution: Visible stock and queue state explain why earnings rise or stall.
observations.recoveryReplay: The player can immediately resume the stock→queue→checkout cycle.

transferablePatterns: Show customer route and queue occupancy in the playfield, not only in helper text.
Make shelf depletion and checkout throughput the readable sources of pressure.
Keep recovery local and replayable: restock, return, serve, repeat.
rejectCopying: Do not copy Monkey Mart names, characters, art, UI geometry, map layout, prompts, or tuning values.
Use the existing original sea-otter beach-market expression and seafood economy instead.
